2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:

Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.

Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: High concern: Out of more than 200 Sub-Saharan African utilities from 42 countries in IBNET, only 75 utilities from 25 countries (235 utility-year observations; 72 utilities and 225 observations in models including public expenditure) had complete data on the 3-year water coverage difference and covariates (PDF pp. 4-5, 9). Within the retained unbalanced panel spanning 1996-2009, 29 of 75 utilities contribute only 1 observation and 22 contribute only 2 observations (Table 7, PDF p. 13), and no imputation or inverse-probability weighting was applied.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Identification relies on lagging explanatory variables by 3 years (Eq. 1, PDF p. 4) and estimating pooled OLS, utility fixed-effects, and utility random-effects models without exogenous policy variation or quasi-experimental identification. Regressing the 3-year change (Y_{t+3} - Y_t) on initial coverage (Y_t) induces mechanical measurement-error mean-reversion and dynamic panel (Nickell) bias in short panels; the Hausman test rejects random-effects consistency (chi2 = 20.74, Table 4, PDF p. 7); public expenditure (2001-05 country average) and ODA/urbanization are measured only at the country level; and critical time-varying institutional confounders such as corruption, tariff structures, and existence of a regulator are omitted (PDF p. 9).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Although the study motivates and interprets its findings around corporatization, performance contracts, donor loan covenants, and regulatory cost-recovery targets (e.g., NWASCO in Zambia), no statute, regulation, contract, or regulatory target is directly coded or measured in the empirical analysis. Instead, achieved accounting O&M cost recovery (operating revenues divided by operating and maintenance costs) is used as an indirect operational proxy, and the authors explicitly note that existence of a regulator had to be excluded due to unavailable data (PDF p. 9), with only a coarse 3-tier jurisdictional dummy (national, regional/state, municipal) added in Appendix C Model h4 (PDF pp. 13-14).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Both the primary exposure (O&M cost recovery) and outcome (3-year change in water coverage) derive from utility self-reported IBNET benchmarking records affected by general quality problems, inconsistent utility ID numbers across years, and figure revisions between the March 2011 and May 2013 IBNET downloads requiring manual matching (PDF pp. 9-10, Note 17). Baseline water coverage exhibits out-of-range values up to 127% and 3-year coverage changes span -81 to +72 percentage points (SD = 18.28; Table 5, PDF p. 12), while O&M cost recovery is distorted by arrears/delayed payments (>2.0 in ~20 truncated observations; Note 13, PDF p. 10) and country-level controls combine 2001-05 averages (public spending) and 2008-2012 projections (ODA) divided by fixed 2005 GDP (Table 2, PDF p. 5).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Water access is measured via utility-reported IBNET water coverage (population with direct service connection or within reach of a public water point as a percentage of nominal population under utility responsibility) and its 3-year difference (Table 2, PDF p. 5). The binary coverage metric omits water quality, hours/continuity of supply, affordability, and household connection versus standpost distinctions (PDF p. 4), and exhibits severe reporting error/volatility including maximum initial coverage of 127% and 3-year swings from -81 to +72 percentage points (Table 5, PDF p. 12).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern (no pre-analysis plan): No pre-registration or pre-analysis plan is reported, and main specifications impose an ex post truncation of O&M cost recovery <= 2.0 (excluding ~20 observations; Note 13 on PDF p. 10 acknowledges that un-truncated linear models yielded negative coefficients). However, transparency is strengthened by reporting nine OLS, fixed-effects, and random-effects specifications in Table 4 (PDF p. 7), inner-fence random-effects Tobit outlier models in Appendix B (Table 8, PDF p. 13), and seven sample/covariate sensitivity models in Appendix C (Table 9, PDF p. 14), alongside a minor reversed significance-level footnote typo in Table 4.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Inclusion into the analytic sample required voluntary reporting and non-missing longitudinal fields in IBNET, reducing >200 utilities in 42 SSA countries to 75 utilities in 25 countries (PDF pp. 4-5), with nearly half of utilities drawn from just three countries (Nigeria = 18, Zambia = 10, South Africa = 8; Table 7, PDF p. 13), rural water schemes excluded by construction (except potential rural inclusion in 3 South African district municipalities tested in Model h5), and ~20 observations with O&M cost recovery >2.0 dropped in main models (Note 13, PDF p. 10). Aggregate sample means were checked against regional benchmarks in Table 3 (PDF p. 6), but utility-level selection bias remains substantial.

domain_ratings.justification: Exposure (O&M cost recovery) is modeled continuously rather than across discrete exposed/unexposed arms, and all observations come from Sub-Saharan African utilities reporting to the IBNET benchmarking database (including within-utility longitudinal comparisons in fixed-effects Model e). However, comparability across the analytic cohort is uncertain because only 75 of >200 IBNET utilities across 25 of 42 SSA countries had usable data, nearly half come from three countries (Nigeria, South Africa, Zambia), utilities span national, state/regional, and municipal mandates, and three South African district municipalities potentially included rural areas (tested by exclusion in Model h5).

domain_ratings.justification: Across all utilities and years in the dataset, the primary exposure (O&M cost recovery) was defined and calculated identically using the normalized IBNET formula: total annual operational (collected) revenues divided by total annual operating and maintenance costs.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 4-5); Note 8 (PDF p. 10)

domain_ratings.justification: While O&M cost recovery is a standard utility accounting ratio in IBNET, its reliability and construct validity are uncertain: IBNET figures rely on utility self-reports with inconsistent utility IDs and changing values across download dates (March 2011 vs May 2013) requiring manual matching (Note 17); temporary fluctuations such as prior-year arrears payments or delayed cost payments created extreme ratios (>2.0 in ~20 excluded observations, Note 13); and achieved O&M cost recovery is an endogenous financial outcome rather than a direct measure of regulatory cost-recovery targets or corporatization mandates.

domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly identify key utility- and country-level confounders, including initial water coverage, infrastructure maintenance status/technical losses (Non Revenue Water), national fiscal effort (on-budget public expenditure for water), foreign aid (ODA), urbanization rate, geographic region, utility size, and utility institutional tier, while also noting unmeasured confounders (corruption and existence of a regulator).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 4-5); Section 4 (PDF pp. 6-7); Section 5 (PDF p. 9); Appendix C (PDF pp. 12-14)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Strategies to deal with confounding stated
domain_ratings.justification: Strategies to address confounding and reverse causality are explicitly stated and implemented: lagging all explanatory variables by 3 years relative to the water coverage change (Eq. 1), estimating utility fixed-effects and random-effects panel regressions to account for time-invariant utility heterogeneity, controlling for baseline coverage, NRW, public expenditure, urbanization, ODA, and sub-regional dummies (Table 4), and running sensitivity models with utility size, institutional tier, per-capita spending/ODA, and exclusion of mixed urban-rural utilities (Appendix C, Table 9). Residual time-varying confounding nonetheless remains high due to omitted institutional variables and country-level/time-invariant fiscal controls.

However, sufficiency of a 3-year lag to capture infrastructure expansion resulting from financial performance is uncertain: Note 12 describes 3 years as a pragmatic compromise to preserve sample size, whereas Section 2b notes that water infrastructure investment horizons typically exceed 20 years.

domain_ratings.justification: Longitudinal follow-up is severely incomplete: out of >200 utilities from 42 SSA countries in IBNET, only 75 utilities from 25 countries (235 observations; 225 in models with public expenditure) had the required 3-year coverage difference and covariates, and 51 of the 75 utilities have only 1 or 2 observations over the 14-year study window (Table 7). Aside from comparing overall sample means of coverage and cost recovery to literature benchmarks in Table 3, the authors do not systematically investigate utility-level predictors or mechanisms of longitudinal non-reporting/attrition.

domain_ratings.justification: No statistical methods to address missing longitudinal observations or panel attrition (such as multiple imputation, inverse-probability weighting, or Heckman-type selection correction) were employed; estimation relies on unbalanced complete-case panel regressions (Appendix B Tobit censoring addresses extreme values among observed cases rather than missing follow-up).

domain_ratings.justification: Although the authors report cluster-robust standard errors, compare OLS, FE, and RE, check cubic/quartic terms, and run Tobit and covariate sensitivity checks, the core econometric specification regresses the 3-year difference (Y_{t+3} - Y_t) on initial water coverage (Y_t) in a very short, heavily unbalanced panel (29 singleton utilities and mean ~3 obs/utility) without dynamic panel GMM or instrumental variables—inducing mechanical measurement-error mean-reversion and dynamic panel (Nickell) bias (initial coverage jumps from -0.38 in OLS to -0.86 in FE). Furthermore, the Hausman test strongly rejects random-effects consistency (chi2 = 20.74, Table 4), yet almost all main and robustness specifications rely on random effects, overlapping 3-year windows induce MA(2) error structure not modeled in RE Tobit, and Table 4 contains an inverted p-value asterisk footnote.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Methodological quality is rated as High concern under the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies. Marson and Savin (2015) assemble an unbalanced longitudinal panel of 75 urban/peri-urban water utilities across 25 Sub-Saharan African countries (235 utility-year observations, 1996-2009, using 1995-2012 IBNET data) to estimate the nonlinear relationship between baseline O&M cost recovery (and its square) and prospective 3-year changes in water coverage. Strengths include transparent reporting of pooled OLS, utility fixed-effects, and random-effects models with cluster-robust standard errors, explicit recognition of nonlinear trade-offs, random-effects Tobit outlier checks (Appendix B), and multiple sample and covariate sensitivity tests (Appendix C). However, serious internal and construct validity limitations persist: (1) severe selection/attrition from IBNET (>200 utilities in 42 countries reduced to 75 utilities in 25 countries, nearly half in Nigeria, South Africa, and Zambia, with 51 utilities contributing only 1-2 observations and no missing-data adjustments); (2) substantial measurement error in self-reported IBNET indicators, evidenced by inconsistent utility IDs across database downloads, out-of-bounds initial coverage up to 127%, and 3-year coverage swings from -81 to +72 percentage points; (3) absence of direct legal or regulatory exposure measurement (achieved O&M cost recovery is an endogenous financial performance ratio rather than a statutory/regulatory target, and existence of a regulator is omitted); and (4) high risk of residual confounding and econometric bias from regressing 3-year coverage changes (Y_{t+3} - Y_t) on baseline coverage (Y_t) in a very short panel without dynamic GMM/IV estimation and relying primarily on random effects despite Hausman rejection (chi2 = 20.74).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Observational longitudinal panel study (unbalanced utility-level panel regression of 75 urban/peri-urban water utilities across 25 Sub-Saharan African countries, 1996-2009 [1995-2012 data], modeling prospective 3-year changes in water coverage via pooled OLS, fixed effects, and random effects)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design, data sources, variable definitions, and sample composition in Section 3 and Tables 2-3 (PDF pp. 4-6) and Appendix A Tables 5-7 (PDF pp. 12-13); regression specifications and main estimates in Section 4 and Table 4 (PDF pp. 6-8); study limitations in Section 5 (PDF p. 9); data matching, sample truncation, and methodological caveats in Notes 8-26 (PDF pp. 10-11); outlier Tobit and covariate robustness checks in Appendices B-C and Tables 8-9 (PDF pp. 12-14).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The empirical analysis tracks a longitudinal panel of water utilities forward over 3-year intervals (t to t+3 across 1995-2012) to examine how a continuous baseline operational characteristic (O&M cost recovery ratio) predicts subsequent changes in water coverage, without a discrete policy/intervention assignment or quasi-experimental comparator structure (such as DiD, IV, RDD, ITS, or matched treated/untreated policy arms). Because it is longitudinal rather than cross-sectional, and observational/exposure-based rather than a non-randomized evaluation of an assigned intervention, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies is the most appropriate instrument.
